opening.headline: To create workflows with triggers and approval steps without code, you need to know the components of Workflow Builder and the roles of Simulation and Publishing.
body: If you're sending a welcome email to a new employee, setting up an appointment, sharing documents, and creating tickets, it's easy for someone to miss a step. It runs automatically in a set order, but requires human confirmation at important steps.

In this class, we'll look at what Gemini Enterprise's Workflow Builder is, how triggers, steps, and actions lead, and where the human verification step comes into play. We then design a workflow using the example of onboarding new employees and distinguish between the roles of simulation and publishing (turning on).
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain triggers, steps, and human intervention steps in workflow builder
The roles of simulation and publishing can be distinguished.

screens.title: Connect repetitive tasks across multiple apps by hand every time
screens.lead: First, read about what new employee onboarding looks like today.

visual.alt: A scene where a person in charge goes back and forth between four apps and handles the same task one after another.
labels: What if I leave it out?

paragraphs: When the HR team receives a new employee's information, the representative sends a welcome email, sets a schedule for the first week, shares necessary documents, and creates equipment request tickets. The order is the same every time, but a person does it manually by going back and forth between the four apps.

With this approach, it's easy to miss a step during a busy week. Missing document sharing can create confusion for new employees who may not be able to see the information they need on their first day on the job. What's more difficult is that there is no record of who did what and how far.

Interactive, question-and-answer tools are not suited to this task. We need a tool that executes in a set order according to the event of a new employee and has people check only in important places. Gemini Enterprise's Workflow Builder is a tool that brings this together without code.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If you automate this task, you need to decide three things: ‘when to start,’ ‘in what order to do it,’ and ‘where to have a person check it.’ At the end of class, check which part each corresponds to.

screens.outro: Now let me think about whether any of my tasks have a set order.

screens.title: Are there tasks that have a set order?
screens.lead: If you first think about each question in your head and then select it, the instructor will organize your thoughts. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: Which of my tasks do I always do in the same order?
items.answer: Tasks that are always in the same order are the best candidates for a workflow. If you can write down your steps, you can move them into steps in Workflow Builder. For tasks where the order changes each time, an interactive tool may be more appropriate.

items.prompt: At which stage does a person make a decision?
items.answer: The human judgment step is where to place human intervention steps such as approval or information requests. The goal is not to automatically run every step, but to stop the flow where judgment is needed.

items.prompt: Does it start happening every time a new email or new file arrives?
items.answer: If an event starts things off, it is a candidate for an event trigger. Triggers can be changes such as new mail, schedule changes, or new files, or you can schedule them to repeat on a schedule.

screens.outro: Now, let’s start by looking at what tool Workflow Builder is.

screens.title: Workflow Builder and two types of agents
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn what Workflow Builder is, what agents it can create, and who can use it.

tabs.label: what kind of tool it is
tabs.body: Workflow Builder is a no-code and low-code tool for creating, managing, and enabling chat agents and workflows in the Gemini Enterprise web app. You can create it with natural language prompts or a visual editor. Construct deterministic or non-deterministic flows with triggers, steps, and actions, and connect to a variety of data sources and tools. Preview and simulate in an integrated test environment, publish, turn on and share, and even schedule recurring runs on a schedule.

tabs.label: chat agent
tabs.body: An agent created to handle specific tasks through conversation. It is primarily non-deterministic because the response depends on the user's input. It can be a single step or multiple steps. It is suitable for open conversations without fixed steps, dynamic tasks where user input leads the flow, question answering, and data inquiry. For example, checking the status of a Jira ticket or summarizing a specific email thread.

tabs.label: workflow
tabs.body: An agent that executes in a sequence of steps or actions and can use both AI automation and human intervention. Logic can be deterministic or non-deterministic. It is suitable for multi-step processing with a set sequence, tasks that require both AI automation and human approval, and complex processing with conditional branching. For example, automating employee checklists across Gmail and Calendar, and creating reports that publish after human approval.

tabs.label: who can write
tabs.body: Workflow Builder allows employees to create their own agents, but within the administrator's policies. The actions and tools available to agents and workflows are limited to the data connectors, tools, and permissions provided by the administrator. To use it, your administrator must turn on the Enable Workflow Builder toggle on the End user features page.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the parts that make up the workflow one by one.

screens.title: Triggers, Steps, Actions: Parts of a Workflow
screens.lead: Select the arrows to cycle through the parts used in the workflow from start to finish.

visual.alt: Workflow structure starting from a trigger and moving through steps to approval and posting.

steps.title: Trigger: Condition that starts execution
steps.body: A trigger determines when to start a workflow. You can schedule it to repeat on a schedule, or start when data in the connector changes. It is an event-based trigger that starts when a new employee is hired.

steps.title: How event triggers work
steps.body: Event triggers poll to detect changes such as new mail, schedule changes, or new files. In other words, rather than reacting immediately to changes as they occur, we check them periodically. Supported connectors include Confluence, Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, Jira Cloud, OneDrive, Outlook, ServiceNow, SharePoint, and Teams.

steps.title: How to set an event trigger
steps.body: Under Agents, select Create agent, select Start manually, and then click 'What should trigger your agent?' Select App event on the screen. You pick an app and select an event for that app, and the trigger is placed at the top of the workflow. The trigger target connector must be connected to your app as a data store.

steps.title: Agent Stages and Connectors
steps.body: By attaching a connector to the agent stage, you can use rewriting tools to send messages and manage history, as well as search in places like Gmail, Jira, and Google Drive. Because it involves writing as well as reading, you need to be careful about which tools you give them.

steps.title: flow control stage
steps.body: This is the step to configure branching, data filtering, and repetition based on conditions. It is used to create branches by sending different document bundles depending on the job category.

steps.title: other parts
steps.body: You can connect an MCP server as a tool in a workflow step or agent step, and even hand off tasks to other expert agents you already have. Workflows can be created or modified using natural language, and execution history is tracked step by step.

screens.outro: Now that you know the parts, let's summarize the concepts of the human verification phase and data connection.

screens.title: Human verification and data linking
screens.lead: When you select or hover over an underlined term, an explanation appears. Check out the human verification steps and data connection structure.

data.text: A workflow can include a Human in the loop step that pauses execution and waits for user input. The Request info step prompts the user for additional information, while the Approval step displays the output and requires user approval before proceeding to the next step. When execution reaches this step, it appears in the Runs tab with a Needs Review status. Meanwhile, the data read by the trigger originates from a data source and is stored in data store, where it is linked to the app. The app then provides users with search results, actions, and agents using data from data store.

terms.tip: A classification of steps that require human input or approval during workflow execution. By expanding this item in the Add step panel, you can add Request info and Approval.

Stop the workflow and ask the user one or more questions. It is used when additional information or confirmation is needed for progress. Write the context in the Message field and set the question and input format.
Stop the workflow and have a human review and approval of deliverables. Because subsequent steps require approval, place them before steps that are difficult to reverse, such as sending or posting.
Runs that are stuck in the human intervention phase are displayed in the Runs tab. Review staff will find and process executions in this state.
This is where data retrieved from the data source is stored. A separate data store is created for each type of item contained in the data source, and the app connects to it and uses it.

screens.outro: Now let’s put the pieces together and design our onboarding workflow.

screens.title: Commentary: Designing a New Employee Onboarding Workflow
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of moving the onboarding task in question into a workflow along with the names of the parts. Select the arrow to move on.

steps.title: Trigger: Starts when a new entry is made in the HR system
steps.body: The starting point is not a person, but an event. The trigger is the creation of a new employee entry in the personnel system. If you can select an event from a supported connector, use an event trigger. Otherwise, use a scheduled trigger that repeats according to a schedule.

steps.title: Agent Steps: Create a Draft Welcome Email and Schedule Instructions
steps.body: Read employee information to create a draft welcome email and first week itinerary. This step is all about reading and drafting, so there's little risk in leaving it to me automatically. The important thing is that nothing has gone out yet.

steps.title: Flow Control: Divide Document Bundles by Job Function
steps.body: Depending on your job, you will need to send different sets of documents. Using a conditional branch, you can create a branch that sends development documents to the development department and sales documents to the sales department.

steps.title: Approval: Sent only after review and approval by the person in charge.
steps.body: Sending mail is an irreversible action that goes out. At the Approval stage just before sending, the email body, recipients, and document bundle are shown to the person in charge. Without approval, the flow is stuck in the Needs Review state.

steps.title: Create tickets and organize parts after shipping
steps.body: Once approved and emailed, you will be directed to creating an equipment request ticket. In summary, the structure consists of one trigger, agent stage, flow control, approval, and finalization stage. The four things that would have been easy to miss are carried out in a certain order, and people stop only at one important place.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: Without an approval step, documents that go to the wrong recipient or job category may go out without verification. Conversely, automation is meaningless if every step is approved. It makes sense to place approval only before the outgoing step.

screens.outro: Now that the design is complete, let's look at the inspection and operation method before turning it on.

screens.title: Commentary: Simulation, Publishing, Versioning
screens.lead: The instructor simulates the designed workflow and explains the turn-on sequence. Select the arrows to advance one step at a time.

steps.title: Simulation: Preview before turning on
steps.body: If you select Start simulation in the Preview tab, your workflow will be simulated in a realistic way. Check the flow by giving input or answering questions. Simulation is a check before turning it on. There is no operational impact yet.

steps.title: Find out in the summary
steps.body: At the end of the simulation, a summary appears. Expand to check whether it really stops at the approval stage, whether the branching by job category is correct, and whether the output of each stage is as intended.

steps.title: Publish: On
steps.body: If all goes well, turn the workflow on with Turn on. From the moment you turn it on, the trigger activates and executes the steps. If you're not ready yet, you can save it as a draft and turn it on later. If simulation is inspection, turning it on is the start of operation.

steps.title: version operation
steps.body: After turning it on, you can create a new version and verify it without touching the running version. If you run into problems, you can revert to a previous version by selecting it from Version history.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Sequence of triggers, steps, approvals, and postings
screens.lead: We will organize the structures seen in this class into one basic sequence.

paragraphs: The basic structure of the workflow is to start with a trigger, go through steps, get human approval in important places, then check with simulation and publish. The first onboarding problem was also solved in this order. The event of a new employee was the trigger, emails, schedules, documents, and tickets were the steps, and the confirmation just before sending the email was Approval.

It also outlines your chat agent and workflow choices. Chat agents are suitable for questions and inquiries that are open through conversation, and workflows are suitable for processing that requires a set order and human approval.

And simulation and publishing have different roles. Simulation is about checking step-by-step behavior and output before turning it on, and publishing (turning it on) is about making the trigger actually work. The two cannot replace each other. Finally, all of this is done within the scope of functions, connectors, and permissions granted by the administrator.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Start with a trigger, process it as a step, get approval on the way out, check it with a simulation and then publish it.

checks.q: What would be better if you want to automatically run email, calendar, document sharing, and ticket creation in a set order every time a new employee is hired?
options: Chat agent that asks questions once in a conversation
Workflows that execute steps in sequence based on triggers
Feature access list in the administrator console
List of apps connected to data store
checks.explain: Workflows start with a trigger and execute specified steps and actions in sequence, making them suitable for repetitive, sequential tasks.

wrong.0: Chat agents are conversational and their responses are often non-deterministic, making them less suitable for automated execution in a set order.
wrong.2: The function access list is a setting that turns on and off available functions, not a tool for creating a task order.
wrong.3: Connecting to a data store prepares the data for the trigger to read and does not define the order of business.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match each section of your onboarding workflow with the parts used
left: Start when a new entry is created in the personnel system
Sending different bundles of documents depending on the job category
The person in charge must view and approve the email before sending it.
checks.explain: The starting condition is Trigger, the job branch is flow control, and the step to obtain human approval is Approval.
checks.intro: Try to organize the concepts and explanations by pairing them. Results are not recorded.

glossary.def: This is a tool to create and manage chat agents and workflows in Gemini Enterprise with no-code and low-code.
The condition that starts the workflow execution. This could be a change in schedule or connector data.
This is a method of executing a workflow by detecting changes such as new mail or new files in the connector through polling.
This is the step to configure conditional branching, data filtering, and iteration.

misconceptions.myth: The workflow always produces the same result.
misconceptions.fact: The response of a workflow can be deterministic or non-deterministic, depending on its overall configuration. For areas where the results need to be fixed, check the configuration and check with simulation.
Event triggers detect changes by polling. Since this is a periodic check, there may be a time gap between the moment a change occurs and the time it is implemented.

misconceptions.myth: Once created, anyone can use it right away.
misconceptions.fact: To use it, the administrator must turn on the Workflow Builder feature, and the tools and connectors used by the agent are limited to the scope prepared by the administrator.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Workflow Builder connects triggers, steps, and actions with no code.
Chat agents are suitable for conversational tasks, while workflows are suitable for automated execution in a set sequence.
Leave human confirmation, such as Approval, at critical steps.
After checking with the simulation, publish it and leave a way to revert to the version.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What are the repetitive tasks in my work that can be divided into triggers and steps, and what are the triggers?
